entries: Orders promise Kesh authority over communities he does not currently control.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Breaking the leadership opens the Ash Road and weakens Tyren’s regional reach.

entries.name: Emmer Hold: The Siege Within
entries: Emmer Hold is technically allied to Bellweather but divided by a commander willing to accept Tyren’s protection.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The party arrives during a political standoff. Loyalists hold the inner yard while the commander controls the armory.
The party can negotiate a surrender, expose the commander’s secret orders, or fight for the armory.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Captain Emmer wants the hold to survive and can be persuaded. Commander Darr Vale believes Bellweather is doomed.

{@b NPC description — Captain Emmer and Commander Darr Vale.} Emmer is a tall dragonborn woman in middle age, with copper-colored scales, one weathered horn tip, dented armor, and a practical cloak; she has the tired expression of someone calculating how many people can still be saved. Darr Vale is an older human man, lean and rigid, with close-cropped white hair and immaculately maintained arms; even at rest he stands like a man waiting for a formation to dress ranks.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: If needed, use {@creature Commander Darr Vale|NCFA} with 4 {@creature Guard|XMM|Guards}.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Darr’s orders instruct him to delay regional aid until Varen Keep is secure.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Resolving the split gives the party soldiers or supplies for the finale.

entries.name: Iron Banner Fort: The Choice
entries: The fort is a professional military force split between Tyren loyalists and pragmatists.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The party can present evidence, challenge the command structure, sabotage Tyren’s artifact, or negotiate neutrality.
Avoid treating every soldier as an enemy.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Haren Vell, the Iron Banner commander, values order and fears chaos more than Tyren.

{@b NPC description — Commander Haren Vell.} A broad dwarf man in late middle age, tall for a dwarf, with iron-gray hair, a squared beard, and dark, well-maintained plate bearing the Iron Banner plainly rather than ostentatiously. His movements are economical and his voice controlled; he gives the impression that chaos itself offends him more than any particular enemy.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: If open combat occurs, use small squads of {@creature Knight|XMM|Knights} and {@creature Veteran|XMM|Veterans}; do not run the entire fort on one initiative.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Haren Vell's command vault contains a Tyren-linked signal device used to receive orders. Destroying, seizing, or exposing it proves the command relationship. This signal device is separate from the sealed planar vessel sought by Doman.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Alliance provides elite troops; neutrality prevents reinforcements reaching Tyren; hostility creates one extra complication in Chapter 17.

entries.name: Transition to Chapter 16
entries: Once the party has enough allies and routes, Perrin Cardon presents a supposedly urgent mission to Zennar Outpost. His betrayal begins the final political crisis.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: {@b Treasure and rewards.} Across the entire regional arc, aim for roughly {@b 12,000 gp} of spendable or saleable party value, not 12,000 gp from every settlement. The Ash Road war chest provides {@b 4,000 gp} in coin and trade bars plus 2 consumables and one rare item. Remaining value comes from alliance payments, trade goods, lawful spoils, and regional rewards. Iron Banner and Emmer rewards are primarily alliance, access, supplies, and at most one rare/very rare permanent item total across the regional arc. Avoid stacking permanent rewards from every settlement.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: These rewards are party totals for the campaign's four-character baseline. Named story relics remain in place; where an older generic treasure quantity conflicts with this section, use this section.

items: {@b Spendable wealth.} 500–1,500 gp total across major resolved sites rather than a separate large hoard at every stop.
{@b Consumables.} About 1 useful consumable per major resolved site.
{@b Permanent magic.} 1 very rare permanent item total across the regional arc, plus up to 1–2 uncommon or rare crafted rewards from allied communities when earned.
{@b Story reward.} Safe routes, allies, intelligence, and military or logistical support for Bellweather.

data.name: Chapter 16: The Zennar Outpost
entries: {@b Recommended level:} 15–16

entries.name: Chapter Overview
entries: {@b Session purpose.} Survive Perrin’s betrayal, preserve proof, and return to a Bellweather where official institutions have been turned against the party.

Now serving as Bellweather's First Councilor, Perrin gives the party an apparently legitimate high-priority mission to Zennar Outpost. The orders are designed to put them where they can be killed or discredited.
The chapter ends with the party outside normal legal protection, relying on allies they earned during the campaign while they gather enough proof to expose Perrin.
{@b Leads onward.} Evidence from Zennar and earlier chapters confirms that Tyren’s central power remains at Varen Keep and that his current host must be separated from the Radiant Well.

entries.name: Running the Chapter
entries: {@b Primary objectives.} Identify the hidden order, escape or turn the outpost, preserve proof.
{@b Player agency.} Expose the message early, negotiate with the outpost, fake compliance, escape, or fight.
{@b Fail forward.} The betrayal cannot hinge on one Investigation roll; the evidence surfaces through orders, testimony, or intercepted communication.

{@b Rest and pressure.} Safe long rests are available back at Ledger House. Inside the active adventure site, resting gives opposing factions time to reposition unless the characters secure a defensible refuge.

entries.name: Table-Ready Purpose
entries: Run this as a political betrayal and survival chapter. The documents Cardon sends with the party are evidence against him. Use {@b Veterans}, {@b Knights}, {@creature Spy|XMM|Spies}, and {@b Mages} rather than a mass garrison encounter. Escape, negotiation, and exposing Cardon are more important than defeating the whole outpost.

This mission occurs after Perrin has become First Councilor and has enough formal authority, administrative allies, and public credibility to send the party away, arrange their deaths, and prepare a legal narrative before they return.

entries.name: Cardon's Public Reassurance
entries: While the characters are away, Perrin prepares the public story before they can tell their own. Notices and statements describe rumors of Council corruption as irresponsible speculation and insist that Bellweather's administration remains stable. His preferred line is familiar:
{@b "Bellweather's recovery remains secure. There is no cause for alarm."}

This is the phrase at its most political. Perrin is not merely calming frightened citizens; he is using reassurance to define dissent as panic and to make legitimate warnings sound reckless. Characters who preserved older Council notices or the Marren Library circular can explicitly point out the repetition when they return. Doing so should matter socially even if it does not automatically prove his crimes.

entries.name: Encounter Guidance
entries: Treat this as political danger as much as combat. Use {@creature Veteran|XMM}, {@creature Knight|XMM}, {@creature Mage|XMM}, {@creature Spy|XMM}, {@creature Assassin|XMM}, and other current humanoid stat blocks according to role. Preserve the diplomatic trap and evidence that exposes Cardon.

{@b Keyed-area encounters.} When a scene and a keyed location describe the same encounter, use the roster and objective in the scene. Creatures listed only in the keyed reference apply when the characters explore that location outside the scene sequence.

entries.name: Perrin's Institutional Position
entries: Perrin enters this chapter as First Councilor, not as an ordinary council member who suddenly has impossible access. The Zennar orders use genuine seals and real administrative channels; the fraud is in the authorization, routing, and purpose.

His clerk-and-merchant network helps him move money, prepare public statements, and create a paper trail that looks legitimate long enough to endanger the party. The betrayal is an abuse of institutions he spent the campaign learning to control.

entries.name: Approaching the Outpost
entries: Zennar is a disciplined stone-and-timber stockade on a defensible rise. A cavalry patrol meets unknown travelers and requests that they enter under escort. The patrol is suspicious, professional, and interested in the party's connection to Bellweather.
Characters can:

items: enter openly as envoys;
inspect the packet before arrival and attempt to reseal it;
approach covertly to observe the post first;
contact a trader, prisoner, or low-ranking soldier outside the walls;
refuse entry and negotiate at the gate.

entries.name: Discovering the Trap
entries: Opening Cardon's packet reveals the betrayal directly. Without opening it, characters can still notice warning signs: the commandant becomes unusually interested in where they are sleeping, guards are assigned as watchers rather than escorts, and staff quietly remove civilians from their corridor. A successful Wisdom (Insight) or Intelligence (Investigation) check gives earlier warning, but the clue is never locked behind one roll.

entries.name: Inside Zennar
entries: If welcomed as envoys, the party receives quarters and a controlled tour. The outpost contains soldiers with different loyalties; not everyone knows about the assassination order. Characters who build rapport can discover that the commandant received instructions from Bellweather that same day.

If the party is detained, they are treated as valuable political prisoners. Their equipment is secured separately. Use imprisonment as a {@b fail-forward sequence} with opportunities for bribery, outside help, forged orders, negotiation, or escape. Do not end the adventure through forced enslavement or an unwinnable mass battle.

entries.name: The Assassination Attempt
entries: If the party remains overnight without exposing the plot, three {@b Veterans} and one {@creature Mage|XMM}, supported by four {@creature Guard|XMM|Guards}, attempt a quiet arrest-and-kill operation. They gain only the advantages they have actually earned through stealth and positioning. Roll attacks and saving throws normally; sleeping characters use the normal 2024 rules.
The attackers withdraw if the operation becomes loud or clearly fails. Most of the garrison believes the disturbance is an external attack, creating confusion the characters can exploit.

entries.name: Getting Out
entries: The party can escape through the main gate, over the wall, through a service route, disguised among a departing patrol, or with help from someone they befriended. Reinforcements arrive as {@b pressure}, not as hundreds of creatures placed on the battle map.

entries.name: Proof Against Cardon
entries: The commandant's copy of the instruction bears Cardon's seal and phrasing. Captured assassins know they were following a written order delivered from Bellweather. Either source is enough to point the party back toward Cardon; obtaining both makes the political case much stronger.

entries.name: Return to Bellweather
entries: Cardon has used the party's absence to shape the story. Public notices describe the envoys as unstable, compromised, or missing and repeat Perrin's familiar reassurance. The party must decide whether to return openly with evidence, enter quietly and gather allies, or force a Council hearing.

entries.name: Scene 1: Perrin’s Mission
entries: Perrin presents sealed Council orders directing the party to Zennar Outpost to secure evidence of enemy coordination.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The orders look legitimate and use real Council seals. Perrin stresses secrecy and speed.
If the party independently verifies them, a clerk confirms the seal but notes the authorization number belongs to a different minor requisition. This is the first chance to suspect a trap.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Perrin is calm and concerned, not theatrical. He wants the party gone before questions spread.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The paperwork is technically forged through misuse of legitimate records, foreshadowing how Perrin weaponizes institutions.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Discovering the forgery early lets the party approach Zennar cautiously but does not cancel the chapter.

entries.name: Scene 2: Approach to Zennar
entries: The outpost looks undermanned because the ambushers are concealed.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Scouts can spot prepared firing positions, fresh horse tracks, and supplies for more troops than are visible.
A friendly-looking sentry attempts to bring the party into the central yard.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The sentry carries a list of the party’s names and descriptions.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: If the party refuses the yard, the ambush begins from less favorable positions for the attackers.

entries.name: Scene 3: Discovering the Trap
entries: Inside the command office are duplicate orders accusing the party of treason and authorizing lethal force.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The party can seize the papers, question a clerk, or search the records room.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Clerk Elin Voss is frightened and did not know the party would be killed. She admits the documents arrived through Perrin’s office.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The records include a prepared public statement blaming the party for unauthorized violence at Zennar.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Elin is a powerful witness if protected.

entries.name: Scene 4: Assassination Attempt
entries: The hidden strike team attacks once the party has enough evidence to be dangerous.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The attackers focus on isolating and finishing individual characters rather than defending territory.
An escape route through the supply tunnel allows a tactical withdrawal.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Strike leader Varek Holt has been promised immunity and money by Perrin. He knows the political purpose of the mission but not Tyren’s plans.

{@b NPC description — Varek Holt.} A lean elf man who appears young by human standards, tall and long-limbed, with close-cut dark hair, a narrow scar across one cheek, plain dark field gear, and no visible insignia. His weapons are positioned for immediate use. He is composed rather than theatrical, speaks only as much as necessary, and keeps shifting so no one comfortably gets behind him.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: Use {@creature Varek Holt|NCFA}, 2 {@creature Warrior Veteran|XMM|Warrior Veterans}, and 4 {@creature Scout|XMM|Scouts}.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Varek carries a payment order routed through a Cardon-controlled intermediary.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Capturing Varek gives direct testimony; killing him leaves documentary proof.

entries.name: Scene 5: Return as Criminals
entries: Perrin moves before the party can return.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Public notices accuse the characters of exceeding authority, killing lawful agents, stealing records, or conspiring with hostile factions depending on what happened at Zennar.
The party’s previous allies determine whether they have safe houses, sympathetic guards, messengers, and public credibility.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Brakkus shelters civilians connected to the party and refuses to hand over guests without lawful cause, but he does not attack the city government on the party’s behalf.
Wern and Bishop Brann demand evidence before taking a public position.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The Zennar orders, Elin, Varek, and financial records are four independent ways to prove the betrayal. The party needs two credible forms of evidence to break Perrin’s position.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: This chapter turns earlier faction relationships into concrete resources.

entries.name: Scene 6: Exposing Perrin
entries: Run the exposure as a political confrontation, not a courtroom simulation unless the players want one.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The party presents evidence to Councilors, the public, allied factions, or all three. Perrin attacks credibility and procedure rather than confessing.

If evidence is strong, Perrin loses institutional protection and attempts to flee or bargain. If evidence is weaker, regional allies and public witnesses can force an investigation that removes his immediate authority.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Perrin believes he used Bellweather’s institutions to preserve order and his own power. He does not reveal himself as a servant of Tyren because he is not one.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Perrin’s betrayal is human political ambition, separate from Tyren’s supernatural domination.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Once Perrin is neutralized, the party can move openly against Varen Keep.

entries.name: Transition to Chapter 17
entries: Evidence from Zennar and earlier chapters confirms that Tyren’s central power remains at Varen Keep and that his current host must be separated from the Radiant Well.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: {@b Treasure and rewards.} Evidence is the primary reward, but the outpost and allied authorities can provide up to {@b 8,000 gp} in diplomatic restitution, recovered payroll, or lawful compensation if the situation is resolved without simply looting the installation. A violent resolution may reduce the liquid payout while still yielding evidence and political leverage. Do not add a separate conventional dungeon hoard.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: These rewards are party totals for the campaign's four-character baseline. Named story relics remain in place; where an older generic treasure quantity conflicts with this section, use this section.

items: {@b Spendable wealth.} No conventional hoard; up to about 1,000 gp-equivalent in diplomatic restitution or recovered value if the outcome supports it.
{@b Consumables.} 1–2 emergency consumables if earned through exploration, negotiation, or recovery.
{@b Permanent magic.} No automatic permanent item. The evidence recovered here is the primary treasure.
{@b Story reward.} Evidence against Cardon interests, political leverage, and the possibility of an outpost alliance.

data.name: Chapter 17: Varen Keep and the Radiant Well
entries: {@b Recommended level:} 16

entries.name: Maps
entries: {@link Player Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/player/varen_keep.webp}
{@link DM Keyed Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/dm/varen_keep.webp}

entries.name: Chapter Overview
entries: {@b Session purpose.} Break Tyren’s control, free or defeat Soren without reducing the finale to a static dragon fight, and decide the fate of the Radiant Well.
With Perrin exposed or politically broken, the party moves against Varen Keep, the center of Tyren’s remaining power.

Victory is not just killing an enemy. The campaign ends with the characters deciding who controls the Well, what political order replaces Perrin’s influence, and what kind of city Bellweather becomes.

entries.name: Running the Chapter
entries: {@b Primary objectives.} Reach Tyren, break control systems/allies, survive the host confrontation, decide the Well’s fate.
{@b Player agency.} Assault, infiltration, exploit internal factions, use recovered lore, or create a political/military coalition.
{@b Fail forward.} Knowledge needed to challenge Tyren has been seeded across Savin Keep, Marren Library, Maren Isle, and Cardon’s records.

{@b Rest and pressure.} Safe long rests are available back at Ledger House. Inside the active adventure site, resting gives opposing factions time to reposition unless the characters secure a defensible refuge.

### ##### Treasure Override By the finale, strong items are appropriate, but avoid a sudden old-school cache. Award at most {@b one major permanent item per character} across the entire castle, with the Radiant Well itself treated as a story object rather than portable treasure.

entries.name: Encounter Guidance
entries: Use the {@creature Adult Bronze Dragon|XMM} as Soren's base stat block. Tyren is represented narratively as the possessing intelligence and mechanically with a limited fiery-aura/possession overlay described in this chapter. For a second phase, use a {@creature Efreeti|XMM} stat block reskinned as Tyren temporarily manifesting in flame if the group needs a level-16 climax. Avoid the Ancient Bronze Dragon stat block for a four-character level-16 party unless the group is unusually optimized.

{@b Keyed-area encounters.} When a scene and a keyed location describe the same encounter, use the roster and objective in the scene. Creatures listed only in the keyed reference apply when the characters explore that location outside the scene sequence.

entries.name: Tyren Alert Track
entries: Start the assault at {@b Alert 0}. Failed infiltration/set-piece objectives, obvious alarms, or deliberately noisy choices can increase Alert by 1, to a maximum of 3. A successful deception or sabotage can prevent an increase when fiction supports it, but Alert normally does not decrease once Tyren knows the party is inside.

items: {@b Alert 0 — Unaware.} No extra complication. The party controls the tempo of the approach.
{@b Alert 1 — Suspicious.} Patrols tighten or one route closes. Add surveillance, a locked approach, or a repositioned patrol, not another mandatory full combat.
{@b Alert 2 — Mobilized.} One outer complication or reinforcement wave remains unless a regional ally or completed sabotage specifically cancels it.

{@b Alert 3 — Full Alert.} Tyren begins the Soren phase prepared. One surviving control node starts active, or Soren begins with one defensive advantage that ends when the party disables the related control focus. Do not add an extra boss encounter.

entries: Alert changes pressure; it never removes routes to the climax, invalidates earlier alliances, or turns Varen Keep into a room-by-room attrition dungeon.

entries.name: Location and Background Details
entries: Varen Keep is the adventure climax. Do {@b not} clear it room by room. Use the source map for geography, then run the keep as a sequence of infiltration choices and 3–5 set pieces that feed the three-phase finale above.

entries.name: Area Description
entries: The outer compound has been cleared for lines of sight. Guards, servants, coerced workers, and Tyren's advisors occupy the surrounding buildings. At the center stands the decaying tower. The bailey has been converted into a thorn maze whose black flowers glow faintly when the Radiant Well surges.

{@b Thorn Maze.} A creature forcing through a hedge must make a {@b DC 15 Dexterity saving throw}, taking {@b 3d6 piercing plus 3d6 poison damage} and becoming {@b Poisoned until the end of its next turn} on a failure. Cutting a person-sized gap requires 30 damage from suitable weapons or tools. Creative magic can bypass the maze normally.

{@b Teleporters.} Four marked spaces connect unpredictably. When a creature activates one, roll 1d4 to determine the destination among the four pads. A character who studies two activations can make a DC 15 Intelligence (Arcana) check to identify the pattern and choose a destination thereafter.

entries.name: Keyed Areas
entries: Only the areas below need full treatment. Other numbered rooms on the map are empty, storage, ordinary quarters, or connective spaces unless circumstances during play make them relevant.

{@b 2. Watchpost.} A {@creature Veteran|XMM} officer and 2 {@creature Guard|XMM|Guards} monitor the outer compound. The alarm can be disabled, forged, or redirected. Capturing the watchpost gives advantage on the party's next infiltration check.
{@b 5. Officer's Quarters.} Contains a fragment of the Radiant Well map, {@b 1,500 gp} in payroll and gems, and one useful consumable. The fragment confirms details learned in Marren Library.

{@b 8. Guard Barracks.} Use 2–4 {@b Ogres} or an equivalent tier-appropriate mixed guard detail. A rigged sand bucket is a visible nuisance trap: DC 13 Dexterity save or 1d4 bludgeoning damage and {@b Blinded until the end of the creature's next turn}.

{@b 10. Warband Barracks.} Eight off-duty members of Tyren’s mixed garrison rest here. If alerted, they use bunks as cover and attempt to hold the corridor until reinforcements arrive. Their effects include {@b 500 gp} in pooled pay and trade bars, a duty roster, and the day’s watch password.

{@b 11. Alen's Quarters.} {@creature Alen Hyam|NCFA} is a mage advisor who has intentionally been fed false information by Tyren. He prefers conversation, surrender, or escape to combat. His notes contain one false conclusion and two useful observations about the Well. Use the current Mage stat block exactly as printed.
{@b 12. Main Gate.} The party can use the password, sabotage the mechanism, climb elsewhere, or force the gate. A frontal breach attracts a manageable reinforcement wave rather than an army.

{@b 20. Servants' Hall and Kitchen.} Coerced workers of mixed species know the day's password and the rhythm of the guard rotations. Freeing them removes one reinforcement from Phase 1 and improves Neighborhoods & Workers reputation.

{@b 22. Records Room.} Ten minutes of focused review reveals the pattern of Tyren's growing political and military influence. A successful DC 15 Intelligence (Investigation) check reveals it immediately and also uncovers a report documenting Cardon's dealings. This evidence matters if Cardon's political fate remains unresolved.

{@b 23. Medusa Chamber.} A captive {@creature Medusa|XMM} has been used as a living security measure. She is furious at Tyren, not automatically at the party. Characters who offer freedom can turn her into a temporary ally or source of information. If combat begins, use the current Medusa stat block exactly as printed.

{@b 27. Smithy.} An armorer ({@creature Veteran|XMM}) and three {@creature Bugbear Warrior|XMM|Bugbears} maintain mundane equipment. They initially assume the party belongs to Tyren’s forces if the characters act confidently. The room contains quality mundane gear and trade stock worth about {@b 1,000 gp}, plus tools useful for sabotaging a control node.

{@b 31. False Tyren Chamber.} An impostor ({@creature Gladiator|XMM} or {@creature Veteran|XMM}) and two {@creature Spy|XMM|Spies} maintain a decoy command room. If exposed, the impostor may surrender and explain the deception. The room holds {@b 3,500 gp} in portable valuables and a counterfeit seal.

{@b 36. Blackstone Shrine.} A small Bane shrine serves members of Tyren's coalition. Use a {@creature Cult Fanatic|XMM}, two {@b Acolytes}, and 4–6 mixed worshippers or soldiers only if the scene adds something. The blessing offered here is coercive magic: DC 15 Wisdom save or the target is {@b Cursed}, suffering disadvantage on saves against fear and charm effects created by Bane's servants until {@spell Remove Curse|XPHB} or similar magic ends it. It never changes alignment, class, or personality.

{@b 40. Jeren's Study.} {@b Jeren} is a rival advisor who believes Tyren may eventually discard him. He can be bribed, frightened, recruited, or exposed. If he betrays the party, he uses his current spellcasting and escapes if possible rather than fighting to the death.

{@b NPC description — Jeren.} A slender tiefling man in his thirties, slightly below average height, with deep red skin, swept black horns, a narrow face, expensive robes under a practical traveling mantle, and carefully arranged jewelry. He has a habit of smoothing one sleeve when nervous and tries to look indispensable even when he is plainly considering betrayal.

{@b 44. Tyren's Audience Chamber.} Tyren may speak through Soren here before the final battle. He offers status and command to test what the characters value. Accepting does not automatically remove player agency; any supernatural control uses the finale's possession procedure and requires the relevant game effect to succeed.

entries.name: Set-Piece Sequence
entries: Choose three to five of the following before Phase 2:

items: {@b Silent Entry:} bypass the gate and disable the watchpost.
{@b Free the Workers:} secure passwords and remove reinforcements.
{@b Turn an Advisor:} convince Alen, Jeren, or the medusa to help.
{@b Destroy a Control Node:} sabotage a Well-linked device in the maze or tower.
{@b Expose the Decoy:} defeat or flip the false Tyren group.
{@b Secure the Records:} recover Cardon/Tyren evidence and Well lore.

entries: Each success removes one complication or grants one concrete advantage in the finale. Failure advances the Tyren Alert Track by 1 but never blocks access to the climax.

entries.name: Phase 2: Soren, the Host
entries: Use an {@creature Adult Bronze Dragon|XMM} as Soren's base chassis. Soren is a victim of possession. Tyren's control gives the encounter environmental effects linked to any surviving control nodes. Characters can damage Soren, but the adventure repeatedly signals that breaking the control is the better solution.

entries.name: Phase 3: Transference
entries: When Tyren is expelled, the entity attempts to move through the Radiant Well's conduit. The party can stop it by combining recovered lore with actions at the Well: sealing runes, breaking a conduit, using a recovered relic, or willingly taking a dangerous temporary burden. This phase is solved by objectives and choices, not by reducing another hit-point total to zero.

entries.name: The Fate of the Radiant Well
entries: After Tyren is defeated, the characters choose what happens to the Well:

items: {@b Destroy it:} removes the immediate danger but loses a source of knowledge and power.
{@b Seal it:} preserves the site while making access difficult and politically contested.
{@b Study it:} creates opportunity and risk; Bellweather must decide who controls the research.
{@b Steward it:} place the Well under a new institution, alliance, or set of rules shaped by the party.

entries: The final epilogue should show the consequences in Bellweather rather than declare one choice objectively correct.

entries.name: Finale Overview
entries: The finale is not a room-by-room extermination. It is an assault on a command center followed by a multi-stage effort to free Soren, stop Tyren’s transference, and decide the fate of the Radiant Well. Let earlier alliances remove or soften obstacles.

entries.name: Scene 1: Approach to Varen Keep
entries: Choose the approach based on alliances and intelligence earned earlier.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Possible routes include the main gate with allied troops, a river approach revealed by Waylen scouts, a service passage from old records, or infiltration using captured signals.
For every major regional ally, remove one outer complication: patrols, artillery, blocked route, or reinforcement wave.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The keyed DM map marks major set-piece areas rather than requiring every room to be cleared.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: The party’s campaign choices materially affect how difficult the assault feels.

entries.name: Reedscale Support
entries: If the Reedscale prisoners were rescued and their river route remains friendly, their guides can remove one environmental/navigation complication on the approach or identify a safe method for handling Radiant Well residue. This is a minor-support benefit and is separate from the chapter's major-alliance benefits.

entries.name: Scene 2: Breaking the Command Network
entries: Before confronting Soren, the party can disable three control nodes in the keep.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The signal chamber coordinates troops. The ritual chamber reinforces possession. The reserve host chamber contains captives selected as possible vessels.
Each node disabled grants one finale benefit: no reinforcement wave, Soren loses one defensive advantage, or Tyren has fewer transference targets.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: Use encounters already listed in the chapter’s keyed areas, favoring {@creature Veteran|XMM|Veterans}, {@creature Mage|XMM|Mages}, and small elite groups rather than mass combat.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Captives confirm that Soren is a bronze dragon being controlled, not a willing tyrant.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Skipping nodes is allowed but makes the final phases harder.

entries.name: Scene 3: Soren, Host of Tyren
entries: Soren confronts the party under Tyren’s control.

{@b NPC description — Soren.} Soren is an immense adult bronze dragon whose normally bright metallic scales have dulled in irregular patches around the head, chest, and joints under Tyren's influence. His movements alternate between the controlled precision of an intelligent dragon and sudden unnatural rigidity, with brief moments when his eyes or voice reveal that the person underneath the possession is still resisting.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Use {@creature Soren|NCFA}; its mechanics are the official Adult Bronze Dragon stat block. Tyren forces him to fight intelligently but cruelly, targeting isolation and control rather than dragon instincts.
The party can damage Soren, disrupt the possession focus, invoke evidence or memories that strengthen Soren’s resistance, or use the laboratory methods learned on Maren Isle.

At the end of each round after the ritual node is disabled, one character adjacent to a control focus can use an action to attempt DC 17 Arcana, Religion, or Persuasion. Three total successes weaken Tyren enough to begin separation.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Soren cannot freely communicate while possessed, but brief hesitation or broken phrases show he is still present.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: {@creature Soren|NCFA} plus environmental hazards from the chapter. Do not add unrelated monsters unless the party skipped outer objectives.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Maren Isle research explains why potential new hosts must be kept away when separation begins.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Reducing Soren to 0 hit points is not required. If that happens before separation, Tyren immediately attempts transference.

entries.name: Scene 4: Transference
entries: When Tyren loses control of Soren, the intelligence tries to enter another viable host.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Any uncontrolled captive, major NPC, or character in the Radiant Well chamber can become a target. If the reserve host chamber was cleared, Tyren has fewer options.
The party can isolate targets, destroy conduits, use protective magic, or redirect Tyren into the Well itself.
Run this as a 4-success group challenge before 3 complications. Arcana, Religion, Constitution saves, protective spells, and creative plans can contribute.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Tyren is a possessing intelligence; destroying one host never guaranteed victory. This is the payoff to clues from Savin Keep, Marren Library, Maren Isle, and the regional coalition.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: On a complication, Tyren briefly controls a target for one turn, triggers a Well surge, or damages the chamber. Do not permanently take a PC away on one failed roll.

entries.name: Scene 5: The Radiant Well
entries: Once Tyren is contained, the party must decide what happens to the Well.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Options include sealing it, placing it under shared civic custody, destroying its access structures, studying it under strict safeguards, or another solution the players devise.
No institution has an automatic right to control it. Present arguments from allies and surviving officials, then let the players decide.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Brakkus argues only that no single person should be able to quietly control something capable of taking away another person’s will. Wern worries about defense. Bishop Brann worries about moral danger. Scholars argue that ignorance is also dangerous.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: The final decision should echo the campaign’s questions about power, ownership, legitimacy, and who bears the risk of rebuilding.

entries.name: Scene 6: Bellweather Afterward
entries: End with concrete consequences rather than a generic victory celebration.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Describe streets the party reopened, people they saved, factions they changed, and institutions they challenged.
Resolve Perrin’s remaining assets and influence according to Chapter 16.
Name which communities remain allied, which precedents govern property, and who oversees the Radiant Well.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: The phrase “There is no cause for alarm” can appear one final time only if it now means responsible confidence rather than denial. The healthier Bellweather listens to warnings instead of suppressing them.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: {@b Treasure and rewards.} Across Varen Keep, place about {@b 15,000 gp} in portable coin, gems, military payroll, art, and other lawful spoils, spread through command quarters and secure caches rather than one pile. In addition, award no more than one major permanent item per character across the entire keep, chosen to fit gaps in existing equipment. The Radiant Well itself is a story object and never portable loot.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: These rewards are party totals for the campaign's four-character baseline. Named story relics remain in place; where an older generic treasure quantity conflicts with this section, use this section.

items: {@b Spendable wealth.} 2,000–3,000 gp in recoverable treasure, rewards, heirlooms, and final settlement.
{@b Consumables.} 3 high-tier consumables appropriate to the finale.
{@b Permanent magic.} 1 very rare signature item. A legendary story item may also appear only when it is central to the finale rather than as routine treasure.
{@b Story reward.} Bellweather's future and the ultimate control, destruction, or stewardship of the Radiant Well.

entries.name: Four Reputation Tracks
entries: Start each at 0; range -2 to +2.

items: {@b Council}
{@b Neighborhoods & Workers}
{@b Merchants & Investors}
{@b Independent Factions}

entries: At +2, grant one meaningful favor per chapter when reasonable. At -2, create one active complication per chapter. Reputation never overrides obvious consequences or roleplay.

entries.name: Perrin Cardon Escalation

items: {@b Minor councilor (levels 3–5).} Useful, polished, and peripheral. He supports practical reclamation and earns credibility by being right about some things.
{@b Restored heir (levels 6–8).} The Weavehouse restores substantial Cardon wealth. Perrin hires protection, sponsors visible civic work, and starts a patronage network.
{@b Administrative patron (levels 8–9).} Marren Library and property disputes teach Perrin how Bellweather's records, clerks, forms, and merchant relationships actually work.
{@b Committee chair (levels 9–12).} Perrin chairs Reclamation and Emergency Works, gaining legitimate access to contracts, requisitions, seals, hearings, and staff.

{@b Dominant councilor / First Councilor (levels 13–15).} Emergency authority and regional politics let Perrin become the formal head of the Council unless the party has already lawfully removed him with extraordinary evidence.
{@b Betrayer (levels 15–16).} Perrin uses genuine institutional machinery to create the Zennar trap, move money through intermediaries, and define the public story before the party returns.

entries: Do not make Perrin openly villainous ahead of the evidence. His rise should be visible, procedurally plausible, and partly earned through legitimate successes. His eventual betrayal is human political ambition and abuse of authority, not service to Tyren.

entries.name: Tyren Reveal Ladder

items: Separate hostile groups share signals and supplies.
The “Boss” coordinates groups that normally compete.
Historical records show the same impossible coordination during Bellweather's fall.
Savin Keep names Tyren and radiant water.
Marren Library establishes host transfer/possession.
Maren Isle independently confirms the Well's consciousness effects.
Regional factions explain how Tyren mixes money, threats, alliance, and supernatural domination.
Varen Keep reveals Soren as the current host.

entries: Never require one roll for any step. If a clue is essential, the party receives it from the correct location/person.

entries.name: Bellweather Change Checklist
entries: After every major expedition show at least two:

items: a physical improvement;
a new business/worker/refugee group;
changing prices or rents;
a property dispute;
a new patrol/gate/route;
a public notice;
a benefit ordinary residents can name;
a cost ordinary residents can name;
Perrin gaining or losing visible influence.

entries.name: Brakkus Boundary
entries: Brakkus Ledgerhelm is a roughly 48-year-old {@b half-orc, level 16 Oath of Devotion paladin of Torm} and retired adventurer. He runs Ledger House because that is the life he chose after adventuring. He is formidable enough to make serious violence under his roof a poor decision, but he is not the party's regular quest-giver, field companion, political leader, or solution to Bellweather's problems. Use his full stat block only when violence reaches him or people under his protection.

entries.name: Reclamation Map State
entries: At the end of every chapter that materially changes control of Bellweather or its approaches, update the campaign map before the party next sees the city.

items: Mark each known area as Secured, Contested, or Unreclaimed.
Move the secured frontier only where Bellweather can realistically defend the new ground.
Add or remove barricades, gates, watch posts, blocked streets, repaired wall sections, and opened routes to show the change physically.
For isolated reclaimed sites, mark a fortified outpost and the secured route connecting it to Bellweather rather than enclosing it within the main perimeter.
Show visible civic consequences of reclamation: workers, reopened buildings, trade traffic, patrol presence, reconstruction, and new access to neighboring districts.
Keep undiscovered enemies, secret passages, hidden objectives, and other DM-only information off the player map.

entries: The map is a campaign-state tool, not static art. A newly printed or displayed version after major victories is part of the reward: the players should be able to see Bellweather becoming larger, safer, and more connected because of their actions.

data.name: Appendix A: Random Encounters
entries: Use these tables instead of rolling directly on the 1988 creature lists. Encounters should reflect the party's current level, and most intelligent creatures should have a motive other than immediate suicide-by-adventurer.

entries.name: Reward Philosophy
entries: No Cause for Alarm uses a four-character reward curve. Treasure should feel generous without turning Bellweather into a magic-item vending machine. Use four reward lanes: spendable wealth, consumables, permanent magic, and story rewards.

Permanent magic is curated. Tie important items to named locations, recovered heirlooms, factions, civic assets, or consequences whenever possible. Consumables and story rewards can be generous because they broaden choices without permanently inflating every combat number.

{@b Superseding rule.} Where this appendix or a chapter's Rewards section conflicts with an older generic treasure quantity, use the newer reward guidance. Preserve named story relics that matter to the chapter, then reduce other permanent treasure if needed to stay near the campaign curve.

entries.name: Permanent Magic Pacing

entries: {@b Attunement guardrail.} Before adding another permanent item, check the likely recipient. If that character already has three desirable attunement items, prefer a non-attunement item, consumable, story reward, gold or valuables, or an upgrade that replaces an existing item.

{@b Level-5 check.} After Kellan's Well, count meaningful permanent items owned by the party. With 0–1, place 2 uncommon rewards across the next two major treasure sites. With 2, add 1 uncommon reward at Koven House. With 3, add 1 uncommon at Koven House or Savin Keep. With 4 or more, no catch-up is needed. Do not award unusable filler merely to hit a number.

entries.name: Permanent Item Selection
entries: When a chapter calls for an uncommon, rare, or very rare item, do not roll blindly from the entire published list. Identify the character who has received the least meaningful treasure recently, check attunement congestion, choose a small set of published items of the correct rarity that fit the location and character, and favor the option that creates a new capability rather than only increasing the character's best number.

Across the four characters, spread rewards among offense, defense, mobility, exploration, spellcasting, healing or support, and social or information utility. Review permanent AC boosts, save DC boosts, extra actions or turns, low-cost flight, summoning items, items that create permanent creatures, technology not already established in the campaign, and unusually strong stacking combinations before placing them.

entries.name: Salvage and Ownership
entries: Bellweather is a reclamation campaign, so not everything found in a ruin is automatically ownerless.

items: {@b Clearly abandoned salvage.} Scrap metal, ruined trade stock, monster hoards, and unclaimed coin can normally be kept or sold by the party.
{@b Identifiable private property.} Marked jewelry, ledgers, family heirlooms, and stolen trade goods can be returned for reputation, favors, a finder's reward, or negotiated compensation.

{@b Civic or religious assets.} Temple relics, guard armory stock, public records, and infrastructure components are normally claimed by the Council, temple, or other steward; the party should receive pay, access, favors, or another meaningful reward instead.

entries: Do not use ownership rules to erase treasure. When the party voluntarily returns valuable property, replace a meaningful portion of the lost cash value with reputation, favors, negotiated pay, access, or another concrete benefit.

entries.name: Story Rewards
entries: When a chapter should feel rewarding without adding another permanent item, use benefits such as temporary free lodging and meals, a Council permit favor, merchant priority or discounts on scarce mundane gear, temple healing or restoration, reclamation-crew support, a safe house, expedition transport, a reliable guide, research access, a difficult faction introduction, or use of a workshop, office, storage area, garden, or dock.

entries.name: Brakkus Ledgerhelm
entries: Brakkus is a roughly forty-eight-year-old {@b half-orc, level 16 Oath of Devotion paladin of Torm}, retired from adventuring and now the proprietor of Ledger House. His mother Elena was a captive librarian in the Ironfang Clan; his father was the warlord Korgak. After Elena's death, Brakkus rejected his father's bloodline, took the surname Ledgerhelm in her honor, and later trained under High Justiciar Vance Halford. Vance gave him the +3 longsword Brakkus named {@item The Appendix|NCFA}.

Brakkus is the stable home-base NPC. He does not need to accompany missions or dominate Council politics. His retirement is a choice, not a loss of ability. Use him to make Bellweather feel inhabited: he remembers names, knows who has been displaced, notices when new money arrives, and can tell when official success looks different from ordinary people's lives.

Do not make Brakkus secretly central to Perrin, Tyren, or the player characters' personal arcs. He offers shelter, introductions, rumors, occasional perspective, and protection of Ledger House. His combat statistics matter mainly if danger reaches his home or civilians under his protection.

entries.name: Cardon and the Inequality Theme
entries: Cardon's ambition should remain clear. His inherited claim, resentment, Council position, private guards, recovered family wealth, and manipulation of public reclamation for private advantage are central to the adventure's theme. He is not wrong because he is wealthy; he is dangerous because he treats public risk and public institutions as tools for restoring what he believes his family deserves.

entries.name: Tyren
entries: Tyren is a different kind of domination: direct supernatural control. This creates useful contrast with Cardon's legal and economic power. The campaign can explore coercion at both institutional and supernatural scales without making every antagonist part of one conspiracy.

entries.name: Version 3 Continuity Locks
entries: {@b Doman.} Doman is the deceptive mage seeking the sealed planar vessel. Commander Haren Vell leads Iron Banner Fort. They are separate NPCs.

{@b Independent threats.} Hessa Vale and Yaren are independent actors. Neither serves Tyren, and Hessa does not work for Yaren. Valen Cemetery does not secretly point to Maren Isle; the poisoned river creates that lead independently.

{@b The Boss.} The title refers to the apparent singular ruler presented by Tyren acting through a host. After the possession reveal, DM-facing text should call the intelligence Tyren; uninformed NPCs may continue saying the Boss. Soren is confirmed as the current host only in the late campaign.
{@b Reedscale.} Rescued Reedscale become a minor ally and can secure the safe river route, but they do not count as one of the three strong alliances required in Chapter 15.

{@b Perrin.} Perrin's political rise is visible and institutional: restored wealth, patronage, administrative network, committee authority, then First Councilor before Zennar. He remains independent of Tyren.
{@b Jarrock.} Rena Dask provides a small 2–3-scene labor subplot that challenges Jarrock's assumptions about class and power without dictating the correct conclusion.

{@b Terminology.} Radiant Well is the only current term; obsolete legacy terminology is removed. Regional relationships use the four established reputation tracks, with regional communities primarily falling under Independent Factions.

entries.name: Downtime Menu
entries: Each character gets one downtime beat between major expeditions unless the fiction is urgent.

items: {@b Gather Information:} one rumor plus a named source.
{@b Build Relationship:} deepen one NPC/faction connection; after meaningful roleplay, gain advantage on one future social check with that contact or shift attitude.
{@b Research:} gain one extra context clue tied to an already-discovered lead.
{@b Work Reclamation:} gain Neighborhoods & Workers goodwill; once per tier, convert this into +1 reputation after a meaningful project.
{@b Craft/Commission:} use current 2024 crafting and local availability.
{@b Train/Carouse:} use current 2024 downtime guidance; success should create a contact, proficiency progress, or useful rumor rather than filler.

entries.name: Ledger House Return Procedure
entries: Every return should take 5–15 minutes at the table unless players linger.

items: Describe one physical change in Bellweather.
Put one familiar person in the common room.
Give one consequence of the party's last choice.
Offer two rumors/opportunities, only one of which needs to be the “next chapter.”

entries.name: Object and Material ACs and HP
entries: Use AC to determine whether an attack damages an unattended object. HP represents how much punishment the object can take before it breaks. In the core object rules, material primarily determines AC while size and whether the construction is fragile or resilient determine HP; the values below combine those rules into a fast DM reference.

The HP columns assume a typical fragile build for cloth/paper/rope and crystal/glass/ice, and a typical resilient build for wood/bone, stone, metal, mithral, and adamantine. Use a lower HP category for thin, rotten, cracked, or poorly made objects and a higher one for unusually thick or reinforced construction. For walls, gates, vehicles, and other very large structures, treat the attacked portion as a separate object and consider a damage threshold when appropriate.

entries.name: Falling
entries: A creature takes 1d6 Bludgeoning damage for every 10 feet fallen, to a maximum of 20d6, and lands Prone unless an effect says otherwise.

entries.name: Jumping

entries.caption: Jumping Quick Reference
rows: Up to Strength score in feet

entries: Each foot jumped costs 1 foot of movement. Landing in Difficult Terrain after a Long Jump requires a DC 10 Dexterity (Acrobatics) check or the jumper becomes Prone. At the DM's option, clearing a low obstacle during a Long Jump can require a DC 10 Strength (Athletics) check. A creature can reach upward an additional distance equal to half its height during a High Jump.

items: {@b Use common sense.} An attack that cannot reasonably damage an object deals no meaningful damage regardless of the attack roll.

{@b Damage Threshold.} If an object has a damage threshold, damage from a single attack or effect below that threshold deals 0 damage; meeting or exceeding the threshold allows the full damage through.
{@b Damage Types.} Objects are generally immune to Poison and Psychic damage. Assign additional resistances, vulnerabilities, or immunities when the material makes them obvious.
{@b Huge and Gargantuan Objects.} Divide very large structures into Large or smaller sections and track damage to the relevant section rather than treating an entire building as one object.
{@b Automatic Breakage.} If an object is extremely fragile and the method is appropriate, allow it to be broken without rolling.

entries: Use this when the environment causes damage and no specific rule gives a value. Choose the damage amount that best matches the severity of the event rather than the source's physical size alone.

entries.name: Exhaustion
entries: Exhaustion is cumulative from level 1 through 6. A creature dies when it reaches Exhaustion level 6. Finishing a Long Rest normally removes 1 Exhaustion level.

entries.caption: Common Environmental Hazards

At 0°F or below, make a DC 10 Constitution save each hour or gain 1 Exhaustion level. Cold Resistance or Immunity automatically succeeds.

At 100°F or above without drinkable water, make an hourly Constitution save: DC 5 for the first hour, +1 per additional hour. Medium/Heavy armor gives Disadvantage; Fire Resistance or Immunity automatically succeeds.

After a number of minutes equal to Constitution score, make a DC 10 Constitution save each additional minute or gain 1 Exhaustion level. Cold Resistance/Immunity or natural adaptation automatically succeeds.
After each hour swimming deeper than 100 feet, a creature without a Swim Speed makes a DC 10 Constitution save or gains 1 Exhaustion level.
Difficult Terrain; entering it for the first time on a turn or starting there requires a DC 10 Dexterity save or the creature becomes Prone.

entries: The efreeti has a 30 percent chance of knowing the {@spell Wish|XPHB} spell. If the efreeti casts the spell for the creature, the efreeti suffers none of the spell's stress. Once the efreeti has cast it three times, the efreeti can't do so again for 365 days.
